MORALITY AND THE CHRISTIAN TRADITION (Section D: Moral Decision-making, Chapter 3)

OPENING QUOTE
- "What good deed must I do to have eternal life?" (Matthew 19:16)

CHRISTIANITY AND MORALITY
- Christianity is about a PERSON: Jesus Christ. Being a Christian means following Jesus' way.
- Questions: do Christians lead a different life to everyone else? Does being Christian make a difference to behaviour? What do we mean by "That was not a very Christian thing to do"?

WORDS VERSUS ACTIONS (two humorous examples)
- The two farms/two houses/two bikes story: a non-Christian asks a Christian if he would give away one of two farms, then one of two houses, because he is a Christian - he says yes. But when asked about one of two bikes, he says "Oh no... Because I have two bikes!" He is generous in theory but not in practice.
- The non-Christian assumes Christians should share what they have.
- The Simpsons: Homer asks Marge, "What is the religion with all the wonderful theories and lovely ideas, but it never works in practice? Oh yes, Christianity!"
- These are NOT good models of Christian living. Assignments suggest researching Sister Stanislaus Kennedy, a saint canonised by Pope John Paul II known for moral courage, or St Francis of Assisi - asking how they respond to God's love and how the Spirit helps them live moral lives.

CHRISTIAN FAITH AND MORALITY: RESPONDING TO THE GOD OF LOVE
- One answer to "Why be moral?" is "to achieve THE GOOD". The good is the goal of all moral effort. To achieve it we must first know what it is.
- For ARISTOTLE the good was HAPPINESS. For HEDONISTS it is PLEASURE. For the person of FAITH it is GOD.
- The Christian's relationship with God shapes how they live and behave. So we look at: what the Bible says about God; what the Church teaches about God; what we learn about God in our faith lives.
- Christianity shapes our moral lives through its teaching on the good and on God, learned from SCRIPTURE and the TEACHING AND LIVED TRADITION OF THE CHURCH.
- God is the GOAL of the moral life for the Christian. Our VISION OF GOD shapes our moral life.
- Christians believe God loves us - no matter what we have done or who we are. God wants us to RESPOND to this love.
- The CENTRAL QUESTION in Christian ethics: "Are we living our lives to the full as God desires?"
- In living a moral life the Christian is RESPONDING TO THE LOVE OF GOD. The Christian lives in the Spirit. God actively helps the person achieve the good through GRACE.
- Living a moral life, "doing the truth", is an active, all-round way of being - much more than obeying a few rules. It is the very way we direct and live our lives.

RICHARD GULA ON LOSING AWARENESS OF GOD
- When morality is not seen as a response to God, it becomes much narrower. Gula says that when awareness of God is lost:
- SIN becomes "the infraction of a rule rather than the turning away from God";
- MORAL ACTIONS become "so many 'works' of moral rightness rather than grateful responses to the goodness of God";
- MORAL DELIBERATION becomes "a computer-like problem-solving rather than a prayerful discernment of what God enables and requires."
- So the Christian is called to live a moral life that leads to God, using REASON AND FAITH - heart and mind, and faith in God.
- Gula also says: "Is recourse to the Bible in moral life possible? Yes. But it is very difficult. Is it necessary? Absolutely."

WHAT IS DIFFERENT ABOUT CHRISTIANITY?
- We expect Christians to act in a certain way ("Wasn't that the Christian thing to do?") and feel let down when Christians do corrupt things.
- A person trying to live a Christian life is guided by SCRIPTURE and the SACRAMENTS:
- Through Christ, the Christian knows what God is like and what God asks.
- Christians are given the HOLY SPIRIT through prayer and the sacraments to guide them.
- Moral character is developed through the Christian VIRTUES of FAITH, HOPE and LOVE.

SCRIPTURE AND MORALITY
- "Moral theology should be more thoroughly nourished by scriptural teaching." (Dogmatic Constitution on Divine Revelation, DEI VERBUM, 24)
- Scripture should be a central source for Christian moral life - where else would a Christian find how God wants us to live?
- The Bible is a best seller that has shaped more lives than any other literature. It gives us the faith of Abraham, the psalms of David, the Good Samaritan, the repentant thief, the Ten Commandments, the Sermon on the Mount.
- The Second Vatican Council called for MORE USE OF SCRIPTURE in moral thought.

DIFFICULTIES IN USING THE BIBLE FOR ETHICS
- The Bible is NOT A CODE BOOK for morality - not a list of dos and don'ts. It is more like a LIBRARY than a book: poetry, proverbs, sayings, history, laws, stories, narratives and personal letters. There is no separate morality section.
- The Bible was written in a VERY DIFFERENT ERA - distant from us in time, geography, culture, language and politics. What can it say directly about human cloning or nuclear war? What do rules on washing hands or sacrificing bulls (Leviticus 1) mean today? How literally do we read them?
- Yet the Bible is a RICH SOURCE of moral guidance: justice, care for the oppressed, love of neighbour, respect for life and property. It is the primary source of stories and images that shape our imagination.
- To become a disciple one must meet God in scripture and enter the Bible story - otherwise one is only a SPECTATOR.

HOW WE USE SCRIPTURE
- PROOF TEXT METHOD: traditionally scripture was used just to back up a teaching, picking a Bible text that fits. We must be careful of this.
- Principles for reading a text:
- What type of book are we reading?
- What is the historical context?
- To whom is the book addressed?
- Then listen to what it says to our lives now: "Where is this happening in my life?" This needs a spirit of REFLECTION and LISTENING.
- Also listen to the wisdom of others: our traditions, the teaching of the Christian community, the advice and experience of our community.
- Example: Matthew 5:38 - "You have heard that it was said, 'An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.' But I say this to you, Do not resist an evildoer. But if anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also." (Question: how would this affect whether a Christian should support a war?)
- Exercises: laws in Exodus 21 and Mark 9:43-48; the command to love (Mark 12:28-34) compared with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:25-37).
- Exodus readings: Exodus 3 (God shares the history of Israel); Exodus 14-15 (God liberates Israel from Egypt); Exodus 20 (God reveals the Law, expressing God's special relationship with the people).

STYLES OF MORAL TEACHING
- LAWS, RULES AND COMMANDS tell us clearly what is prohibited, e.g. "Thou shalt not kill."
- STORIES with powerful images, e.g. the Good Samaritan. They stay with hearers and influence behaviour.
- Some texts see morality as RULES TO BE OBEYED; others as RESPONDING TO GOD'S LOVE and BECOMING A NEW PERSON.

THE COVENANT: CONTEXT - THE PEOPLE OF GOD
- The starting point for biblical authors is GOD: the God who CREATES (Genesis) and the God who SAVES (Exodus).
- One creator God, still involved with people, who gives freedom and cares deeply. God's saving actions are remembered in song and story.
- Values of the people of Israel: THE FAMILY, THE LAND and LIBERTY - from their history as slaves promised the land of their inheritance.
- Their relationship with God is summed up in the COVENANT.

THE COVENANT
- From the Hebrew word BERITH, meaning TO BIND or BOND. It bonds Israel to God in a special way.
- Covenants in the Hebrew Scripture are INITIATED BY GOD, NOT NEGOTIATED. They express God's GRACE. The covenants at SINAI and SHECHEM (Joshua 24) also put OBLIGATIONS on the people.
- The Covenant is a basic motif throughout the whole Hebrew Scripture.
- Characteristics:
- initiated by God; an act of MERCY and GRACE;
- more than a contract: it sets up a kind of BLOOD KINSHIP between the two parties; the word for family loyalty is also used for loyalty to the Covenant;
- it gives a MOTIVE for observing the Law (Deuteronomy 4:23).
- Repeated phrase: "I will be your God, and you will be my people." (Ezekiel 37:27)
- The people's behaviour is judged by: have they kept the Covenant? Are they living as God's people?
- The chief moral concern is the people's RELATIONSHIP WITH GOD. God calls; the people respond. God makes an offer that can be accepted or refused.
- Covenant with Abraham: Genesis 15-17 ("On that day the Lord made a covenant with Abram", Genesis 15:18).
- Covenant with Moses at Sinai: Exodus 19:1-8 ("if you obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession out of all the peoples", Exodus 19:5).
- Marriage is also called a covenant.

INFLUENCES ON THE COVENANT
- The Israelites probably learned legal traditions from their more sophisticated CANAANITE neighbours after entering the Promised Land, and from common NEAR EASTERN laws and customs.
- The COVENANT CODE (Exodus 20:22-23:33) has the most parallels to ancient laws. It is attributed to Moses.
- Laws were in CASE FORM: "If this action happens, then this is the punishment."
- Example - the HAMMURABI LAWS: "If a man strikes his father, they shall cut off his hand." (Hammurabi Laws, 195)
- HAMMURABI was King of BABYLON, ruling from about 1795 to 1750 BCE.

INTERPRETING THE COVENANT
- PRIESTS, PROPHETS and WISE PEOPLE could interpret it - a broad teaching authority.
- Covenant and sin: sin becomes a BREAKING OF RELATIONSHIP rather than a legalistic notion of breaking laws.
- Covenant and contract: a covenant emphasises the RELATIONSHIP between the parties, not just the obligations.
- Covenant and image of God: God loves and saves. The Commandments are the people's way of RESPONDING to that love, NOT EARNING it. The primary claim: God loves us without our having done anything to deserve it (Exodus 19:4-5).
- Reflection: many grow up with an image of God as JUDGE - is this the God of the Covenant? Real love is not a contract; it is more like a covenant.

THE TEN COMMANDMENTS: THE DECALOGUE
- Recorded TWICE: EXODUS 20:2-17 and DEUTERONOMY 5:6-21.
- The CCC (Part Three, end of Section One) gives them with a traditional catechetical formulation.
- The list as given in the chapter:
- I am the Lord your God who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.
- You shall have no other gods besides me.
- You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain.
- Remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy.
- Honour your father and your mother.
- You shall not kill.
- You shall not commit adultery.
- You shall not steal.
- You shall not bear false witness against your neighbour.
- You shall not covet your neighbour, his possessions or his wife.
- Since the time of ST AUGUSTINE the Commandments have been taught to people preparing for baptism - ten laws were easy to teach, you could count them on your fingers!
- Around the FIFTEENTH CENTURY the custom arose of expressing them in RHYMED FORMULAE.
- Many catechisms, including the modern CCC, use the Commandments as a structure to teach morality.

DIFFERENT LISTINGS
- GREEK CHURCH (probably the most accurate): worshipping false gods and images are SEPARATE first two commands; coveting neighbour's house, wife and possessions COMBINED into the last.
- LATIN CHURCH: follows ORIGEN's and AUGUSTINE's list.
- MODERN JEWISH LIST: "I am the Lord your God" is number ONE, and the ninth is collapsed into the tenth.
- It took many centuries for the ten to be brought together as a list. Even in Jesus' time there was no listing as we know it now.
- The SHEMA (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) - a precious Jewish text that puts the commands in the context of how to love God.

CONTEXT OF THE DECALOGUE: COVENANT
- The Commandments are PART OF THE COVENANT. God has saved the people and entered a new relationship with them.
- They are rules of behaviour similar to many Near Eastern law collections.
- They are NOT JUST ETHICAL LAWS - THEY ARE RELIGIOUS. Prohibiting stealing and keeping the Lord's Day holy are part of the same code.
- They are followed AS A UNIT: they integrate LOVE OF GOD and LOVE OF NEIGHBOUR. Religious life and social life are one.
- "Ten words" (DABAR = word) that show how to live free from the slavery of sin.
- "The Decalogue is a path of life." (CCC, 2057)
- They express, in shorthand, the meaning of being a COVENANT PEOPLE.

SUMMARY
- God is the goal of the moral life for the Christian; faith shapes one's ethical vision.
- Traditionally Catholic ethics based its teaching on the Natural Law. Vatican II called for renewed study of scripture.
- Care is needed using scripture in ethics because of different styles of literature.
- The Covenant expresses God's grace and places obligations on God's people, summed up in the Ten Commandments (the Decalogue).
- "Faith informing reason and reason informing faith."

KEY TERMS
- Reason and Faith: the Christian uses both mind and faith in God to live a moral life leading to God.
- The Covenant: the bond (berith) initiated by God between God and Israel, expressing grace and placing obligations on the people.
- The Decalogue: the Ten Commandments ("ten words"), the obligations of the Covenant, found in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5.

rows.prompt: Give two difficulties in using the Bible in ethics today.
rows.model_answer: The Bible is not a code book of dos and don'ts but a library of different types of writing, with no separate morality section. It was also written in a very different era, distant in time, culture and language, so it does not speak directly about issues like cloning or nuclear war.

rows.prompt: Describe two styles of moral teaching in the Bible, with an example of each.
rows.model_answer: Laws, rules and commands tell us clearly what is prohibited, for example 'Thou shalt not kill.' Stories with powerful images teach moral lessons that stay with the hearer, for example the Good Samaritan.

rows.prompt: List three characteristics of the Covenant in the Hebrew Scripture.
rows.model_answer: It is initiated by God as an act of mercy and grace. It is more than a contract, setting up a kind of blood kinship between God and the people. It gives a motive for keeping the Law: 'I will be your God, and you will be my people.'

rows.prompt: What image of God is shown in the Covenant?
rows.model_answer: The God of the Covenant loves and saves. The Commandments are the people's way of responding to that love, not of earning it. God loves us without our having done anything to deserve it - a different image from God as Judge.

rows.prompt: What is the link between the Covenant and the Decalogue?
rows.model_answer: The Commandments are part of the Covenant: God saved the people and entered a new relationship with them, and the Decalogue sums up the obligations of that relationship. They express in shorthand what it means to be a covenant people.

rows.prompt: 'Is recourse to the Bible in moral life possible? Yes. But it is very difficult. Is it necessary? Absolutely.' (Richard Gula). Discuss. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Using the Bible in moral life is necessary. Dei verbum 24 says moral theology 'should be more thoroughly nourished by scriptural teaching', and Vatican II called for more use of scripture. Where else would a Christian find how God wants us to live? The Bible has shaped more lives than any other book, giving us Abraham's faith, David's psalms, the Good Samaritan, the Ten Commandments and the Sermon on the Mount. It teaches justice, care for the oppressed, love of neighbour and respect for life and property, and its stories shape our imagination. To be a disciple one must enter the Bible story or remain a spectator. But it is difficult. The Bible is not a code book of dos and don'ts; it is a library of poetry, history, laws, stories and letters with no morality section. It was written in a very different era, so it says nothing directly about cloning or nuclear war, and rules on washing hands or sacrificing bulls (Leviticus 1) are hard to apply. There is also the danger of the proof text method, picking a verse to back up a teaching. So we must ask what type of book it is, its historical context and to whom it is addressed, then listen to what it says to our lives, along with the wisdom of the Christian community.

rows.prompt: Explain the meaning and characteristics of the Covenant in the Hebrew Scripture and its importance for morality. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The word covenant comes from the Hebrew 'berith', meaning to bind or bond. It bonds the people of Israel to God in a special way and sums up their relationship with God, who creates (Genesis) and saves (Exodus). Covenants are initiated by God, not negotiated; they are acts of mercy and grace. At Sinai and Shechem (Joshua 24) they also place obligations on the people. The Covenant is more than a contract: it sets up a kind of blood kinship, and the word for family loyalty is used for loyalty to it. It gives a motive for keeping the Law (Deuteronomy 4:23), summed up in 'I will be your God, and you will be my people' (Ezekiel 37:27). Examples are the covenant with Abraham (Genesis 15-17) and with Moses at Sinai (Exodus 19). For morality, the chief concern becomes the people's relationship with God: God calls and the people respond. Behaviour is judged by whether they have kept the Covenant and live as God's people. Sin becomes a breaking of relationship, not just a broken rule. The Commandments are a response to God's love, not a way of earning it, because God loves us without our deserving it.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: berith; initiated by God; grace and mercy; obligations (Sinai, Shechem); blood kinship; motive for Law; Ezekiel 37:27; Abraham and Moses; relationship as chief moral concern; sin as broken relationship; covenant vs contract; responding not earning.

rows.prompt: Outline the place of the Decalogue in the moral life of the believer. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The Decalogue, or Ten Commandments, is found twice in scripture: Exodus 20:2-17 and Deuteronomy 5:6-21. The commandments include having no other gods, keeping the Sabbath holy, honouring father and mother, and not killing, committing adultery, stealing or bearing false witness. They are part of the Covenant: God saved the people and entered a new relationship with them, and the commands show how to live in that relationship. They are not just ethical laws but religious ones - not stealing and keeping the Lord's Day holy belong to the same code. They are followed as a unit, joining love of God and love of neighbour, so religious and social life are one. They are 'ten words' (dabar) showing how to live free from the slavery of sin; the CCC (2057) calls the Decalogue 'a path of life'. Since St Augustine they have been taught to those preparing for baptism, and many catechisms, including the CCC, use them to structure moral teaching. The listing differs: the Greek Church separates false gods and images, the Latin Church follows Origen and Augustine, and the Jewish list makes 'I am the Lord your God' the first. The Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4-9) places them in the context of loving God.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: Exodus 20/Deuteronomy 5; examples of commandments; part of Covenant; religious not only ethical; a unit - love of God and neighbour; dabar; CCC 2057; St Augustine and baptism; catechisms; Greek/Latin/Jewish listings; Shema.

rows.prompt: What influences shaped the laws of the Covenant? Refer to the Covenant Code and the Laws of Hammurabi. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: The Israelites probably learned and developed many legal traditions from their more sophisticated Canaanite neighbours after entering the Promised Land. They were also influenced by common Near Eastern laws and customs. The Covenant Code, found in Exodus 20:22-23:33 and attributed to Moses, has the most parallels to ancient laws. Its laws are written in case form, the common way of teaching law in other cultures: if this action happens, then this is the punishment. A good example is the Laws of Hammurabi, King of Babylon, who ruled from about 1795 to 1750 BCE: 'If a man strikes his father, they shall cut off his hand' (Hammurabi Laws, 195). The Decalogue itself is a list of rules similar to many Near Eastern law collections, though placed within Israel's relationship with God.
rows.marking_scheme: Canaanite and Near Eastern influences 3 marks; Covenant Code reference and Moses 2 marks; case form explained 2 marks; Hammurabi details and example 3 marks.

rows.prompt: 'Faith informing reason and reason informing faith.' Explain how Christian faith shapes a person's moral life. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: For the Christian, the good that all moral effort aims at is God, not just happiness (Aristotle) or pleasure (hedonists). Christians believe God loves them whatever they have done, and they live morally as a response to that love, helped by God's grace and living in the Spirit. The central question is: are we living our lives to the full as God desires? Morality is an all-round way of living, not just obeying rules. Richard Gula warns that without God, sin becomes breaking a rule and moral decisions become computer-like problem-solving instead of prayerful discernment. So the Christian uses both reason and faith, heart and mind. They are guided by scripture and the sacraments, receive the Holy Spirit through prayer, and grow in the virtues of faith, hope and love.
rows.marking_scheme: The good as God 2 marks; responding to God's love/grace 2 marks; Gula's point 2 marks; reason and faith 2 marks; scripture, sacraments, Spirit, virtues 2 marks.
